messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lukas's world had been shattered six months ago when his younger brother was brutally assaulted by a group of strangers in their neighborhood. The event still felt like a nightmare from which he couldn't wake up. People acting suspiciously on the street made him immediately tense, as if they might be part of another gang waiting to pounce. Comments about family or even innocuous remarks about his brother's favorite hobbies sent Lukas into a spiral of anxiety, transporting him back to that fateful evening. As he struggled to cope with these triggers, Lukas found himself avoiding anything that might remind him of the event – TV shows, movies, and even social media. He became increasingly withdrawn, afraid of being alone in a room or building, where his mind would inevitably wander back to the assault. In desperate attempts to release overwhelming feelings, he started self-harming, inflicting physical pain on himself as a twisted way to regain control over his emotions. However, these avoidance strategies only seemed to fuel Lukas's perception of threat. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard, making him jump or flinch in anticipation of another attack. Sleep became elusive, as every creak and groan in the night sounded like footsteps outside his door, signaling potential danger. Flashbacks began to haunt him – he would suddenly feel himself back at the scene of the crime, re-living the horror of that evening. Memories of the event lingered vividly, triggered by specific body parts or smells reminiscent of that night. When Lukas closed his eyes, the images came flooding back like photographs in his mind, leaving him shaken and disoriented. He struggled to verbalize what had happened, as if the words themselves would unleash a torrent of emotions he couldn't contain. As time passed, Lukas began to doubt his own resilience. His body seemed to be constantly on high alert, responding to every perceived threat as if still in danger, even when he was safe at home with his wife. He felt no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him – enjoying time outdoors or simply being present for loved ones. Self-doubt crept in, and Lukas became convinced he couldn't rely on himself to navigate these treacherous emotions. This crippling self-perception only intensified his reactivity to triggers, creating a vicious cycle of avoidance and threat perception. Every flashback sent him deeper into the trenches of self-blame and hopelessness. His maladaptive strategies – avoidance and self-harm – further entrenched these negative appraisals, reinforcing the notion that he was no longer capable or trustworthy. As Lukas's symptoms worsened, his relationships began to fray. His wife grew concerned about his increasing isolation and self-destructive tendencies. She encouraged him to seek help, but Lukas felt trapped in this nightmarish cycle, unsure how to break free. It wasn't until he realized that his avoidance was not only failing to protect him but also pushing away the people he loved that Lukas finally found the courage to reach out for support. With a sense of desperation and trepidation, Lukas began therapy, hoping to find a way to silence the cacophony of memories, fears, and doubts that had taken over his life. Though the journey ahead seemed daunting, he knew it was time to confront the darkness head-on – for himself, for his brother's memory, and for the sake of those who cared about him most.
